lines.text: The seven days of the week and twelve months of the year form the backbone of how English speakers organize time. The week begins with Monday in British convention (Sunday in American). Each day carries cultural associations: Monday is often dreaded as the start of the working week, Wednesday marks 'hump day' (the midweek point), Friday brings relief ('TGIF — Thank God It's Friday'), and the weekend — Saturday and Sunday — is for rest and leisure. The twelve months follow the Gregorian calendar. January starts the new year, often associated with resolutions and fresh starts. February is the shortest month and contains Valentine's Day. Spring arrives in March or April, summer peaks in July and August, autumn colours appear in September and October, and winter settles in by November and December. Dates are written differently in British and American English: 25th August 2026 (British) vs August 25, 2026 (American). Ordinal numbers are essential for dates: first, second, third, fourth, and so on. The days of the week and months are always capitalised in English — a common mistake for learners whose languages don't follow this rule. Prepositions of time matter too: 'on' for days (on Monday), 'in' for months (in March), and 'at' for holidays (at Christmas).

lines.text: English day names come from Norse and Roman mythology: Monday (Moon), Tuesday (Tyr), Wednesday (Odin/Woden), Thursday (Thor), Friday (Freya), Saturday (Saturn), Sunday (Sun). This mythology connection is unique to Germanic languages.

lines.text: British format: DD/MM/YYYY (25/08/2026). American format: MM/DD/YYYY (08/25/2026). This causes real confusion internationally — 03/04/2026 is 3rd April in Britain but March 4th in America. Always write month names to avoid ambiguity.

lines.text: 'Fortnight' (fourteen nights = two weeks) is a common British English word that Americans rarely use. 'I'm going on holiday for a fortnight' is natural in British English. Americans would say 'two weeks' instead.

lines.text: In the UK, public holidays are called 'bank holidays' (banks close). Key ones: New Year's Day, Easter Monday, Early May, Spring, Summer bank holidays, Christmas Day, Boxing Day (26 Dec). The US calls them 'federal holidays'.
